summary:
Teletubbylanders is an interactive, end-to-end Space Mission Design Game that challenges individuals or teams of up to four players to conceptualize, architect, and operate complete space missions across six aerospace scenarios and a sandbox mode.

Existing educational tools typically isolate orbital mechanics, rocket launches, or satellite components, leaving a gap in understanding how real mission teams manage coupled systems trade-offs. Teletubbylanders bridges this gap by linking five core subsystems: Target Orbit, Launch Vehicle, Spacecraft Bus & Power, Scientific Instruments, and Communications & Ground Networks, through live resource telemetry and an interactive simulation engine. Upgrading a high-yield sensor immediately ripples across wet mass, rocket lift margins, solar flux and eclipse battery endurance, pointing stability, data buffer capacity, and budget. Players can collaborate across four specialized crew roles (Mission Director, Principal Investigator, Chief Engineer, and Flight & Comms Officer) with cross-role trade-off negotiations, or compete head-to-head as rival agencies solving the same mission objective.

By pairing plain-English causal explanations, live spacecraft schematics, mid-mission anomalies, and root-cause post-mission reports with iterative design comparison, Teletubbylanders turns complex aerospace systems engineering into an accessible, hands-on learning experience.
details:
1. What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

Teletubbylanders is an interactive, end-to-end Space Mission Design & Systems Engineering Simulator organized into a five-page Mission Control workflow:

  1. Mission Control Hub (Overview): Players choose from five realistic aerospace scenarios (Wildfire & Urban Thermal Sentinel, Polar Ice & Sea-Level Altimeter, Global Disaster Relay, Lunar South Pole Ice Prospector, and Mars Atmospheric Escape Orbiter) or configure a custom sandbox contract with user-defined orbits, budgets, science goals, and mission durations.
    • Solo Mission Director (benchmarked against AI rival contractors),
    • 4-Player Co-Op Crew Command (dividing Comms Officer seats with optional strict role locks, engineering handoff requests, and joint Launch Readiness Review sign-offs), and
    • Competitive Space Race (2–4 rival space agencies independently designing, locking bids, and flying spacecraft for the same contract).
  2. Live Flight Operations Theater (Flight Ops): Runs a multi-year orbital simulation on an HTML5 Canvas with adjustable time-warp (1x, 2x, 5x), modeling launch ascent, sunlit charging arcs, planetary eclipse battery drain, ground station downlink passes, and interactive mid-mission anomalies (such as X-class solar flares, target-of-opportunity bursts, and memory saturation).
  3. Debrief, Iteration Matrix & Leaderboard (Analytics): Generates a root-cause engineering report explaining why a mission succeeded or failed, allows side-by-side comparison of up to four saved design iterations, and ranks crews and agencies on a competitive leaderboard.

2. What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Systems-Level Understanding Over Isolated Facts: Instead of teaching orbital mechanics, rocket propulsion, or satellite power in isolation, every choice visibly ripples across all other subsystems.
  • Safe, Rapid Engineering Iteration: Students and aspiring engineers can test risky hypotheses, experience failures (such as eclipse brownouts or data packet loss), diagnose root causes, and iterate designs within minutes.
  • Accessible Across Skill Levels: Four difficulty tiers (Cadet, Engineer, Director, and Sandbox), plain-English causal advisor alerts, and a built-in Space Systems Field Guide make complex aerospace concepts intuitive for beginners while preserving rigorous trade-offs for advanced learners.
  • Authentic Team Negotiation: Co-op roles mirror real NASA/ESA mission teams, encouraging communication when a scientist's high-power radar conflicts with the engineer's mass/power budget or the comms officer's downlink capacity.

3. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

The intended impact of Teletubbylanders is to bridge the gap between textbook aerospace theory and real-world mission systems engineering. By letting learners experience how scientific ambition must be balanced against physical, financial, and operational constraints, the project fosters systems thinking, collaborative problem-solving, and STEM engagement for students, classrooms, hackathons, and space enthusiasts—requiring zero installation or specialized hardware.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and modern JavaScript (ES6+).
    • HTML5 <canvas> 2D API for real-time orbital geometry, eclipse shadow cones, sunlit charging arcs, rocket ascent curves, and ground-station downlink beams.
    • Dynamic Inline SVG for the live spacecraft digital twin that physically morphs its bus chassis, solar wings, nuclear RTG fins, high-gain dishes, and mounted instruments as players build.
  • Audio: Procedural Web Audio API synthesizer generating tactile UI feedback, launch ignition tones, and anomaly alerts without external sound files.
  • Architecture & Hardware: Engineered as a lightweight, self-contained single-page web application (orbital_architect.html) that runs smoothly in any modern desktop or mobile browser on standard consumer laptops, tablets, or classroom Chromebooks.

5. How Is the Project Creative?

  • Live Morphing Digital Twin: Rather than static menus, the spacecraft SVG schematic dynamically reconfigures its physical geometry swapping solar arrays for angled plutonium RTG radiator fins or parabolic dishes for optical laser terminals as parts are clicked.
  • Dual Collaborative & Competitive Gameplay: Combines asymmetrical 4-role crew cooperation (complete with cross-role trade-off alerts and LRR sign-offs) with a head-to-head Space Race contracting mode and AI rival aerospace firms.
  • Interactive Mid-Mission Anomalies: Flights are not passive cutscenes; real-time space weather storms, wheel friction spikes, and transient science events pause telemetry and require role-specific tactical decisions.
  • Causal Engineering Advisor: Translates mathematical formulas (such as inverse-square solar flux loss at Mars or free-space path loss) into actionable, human-readable cause-and-effect explanations.

6. What Factors Did the Team Consider?

  • Physical Realism vs. Playability: We modeled authentic aerospace constraints—the Tsiolkovsky rocket payload drop-off to higher orbits, inverse-square solar flux ($43% at Mars), eclipse battery depth-of-discharge, pointing jitter in arcseconds, and Van Allen radiation belts—while compressing multi-year missions into engaging 15–20 second interactive simulations.
  • No Single "Perfect" Solution: Every scenario supports multiple viable architectures (e.g., pairing a heavy armored bus with solar Mega-Arrays vs. a lighter bus with a nuclear RTG), rewarding thoughtful trade-offs rather than rote memorization.
  • Usability & Classroom Readiness: Because teams may play either around one laptop (pass-and-play) or over screen-share, we included toggleable Strict Role Locks, quick trade-off request buttons, persistent top-level resource bars, and a zero-setup single-file deployment.
